Date: 2026-04-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Location: Zoom
Meeting type: POC weekly checkpoint
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood CSM partial), Alex Rivera (CTO, Crownline), Priya Shah (Infra Lead), Michael Ortiz (ML Eng), Sara Nguyen (Product)
summary: Mid-poc sync focused on latency/throughput delta vs their incumbent (OldVendorAI). Discussed routing decisions, batch sizing, KV cache warmup, and a focused quantization test. Agreed on next steps: shared latency spreadsheet, run 1k qps customer test, Redwood to try a 4-bit quantized pass with lower batch size and TTL KV pre-warm. Pricing update and SOC2 stakeholder availability action items captured.
topics: Tail and P95 latency anomalies observed on 512 token workloads
Routing policy: prefer low-latency pool for priority traffic
Quantization tradeoffs: 4-bit vs 8-bit impact on throughput and hallucination risk
KV prefix cache and warmup strategy
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay, hi everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call, um, Alex you there?
[00:07] Alex Rivera: yeah I'm here, hey Maya, hey Ethan. Sorry had a quick sprint meeting ran a bit over.
[00:12] Ethan Ross: no worries, thanks for making time. Today we want to go over the week five bench numbers and a couple tuning knobs. We've got the comparative sheet to OldVendorAI, and a couple anomalies on the 512 token path.
[00:25] Priya Shah: quick note, we're running tests on our staging VPC so network is stable, but we've seen occasional bursts that spike tail latencies. Not sure if it's net or routing.
[00:36] Maya Chen: okay good callout. The sheet we sent has per-route percentiles, and we flagged the p99 excursions.
[00:43] Michael Ortiz: one thing — the p95 for Redwood Dedicated was consistently 48 ms lower than OldVendor on the 128 token tests, but for 512 tokens p95 jumps and sometimes Redwood is actually slightly slower, weird.
[00:58] Ethan Ross: yeah that's the thing we wanted to unpack — it looks like sequence-length dependent kernel selection plus batching thresholds are shifting behavior. For short sequences we get better kernel dispatch, but once kv cache populates and batching starts, some of the continuous batching heuristics increase queueing.
[01:18] Alex Rivera: so are you saying the batching is hurting us for longer sequences? We thought batching always helped throughput.
[01:24] Ethan Ross: it generally does for throughput, yes, but if your latency SLO is tight and the traffic pattern has many mid-length requests, batching can add queue delay. We experimented with smaller max-batch size for the low-latency pool and that reduced p95 at the cost of tokens/sec.
[01:38] Priya Shah: can you quantify the tokens/sec hit? We want a rough number.
[01:44] Ethan Ross: on that test moving max-batch from 64 to 16 dropped throughput by ~17% on our harness but p95 improved by 38% for 512 tokens. Those are noisy though.
[01:58] Sara Nguyen: is that from the hosted pool or the dedicated slots?
[02:02] Ethan Ross: dedicated slots environment, using our standard ded-rt runtime. On hosted we can route to a lower-cost model variant which has slightly higher median latency but better unit cost.
[02:13] Alex Rivera: hmm, cost vs latency again. Our product team wants sub-200ms p95 for user facing queries.
[02:20] Maya Chen: right, and that's why we're recommending a routing policy: critical traffic to low-latency dedicated pool with smaller batch caps and prefix cache pre-warm; background batchable jobs to higher-throughput capacity.
[02:32] Michael Ortiz: about the prefix cache — we've noticed cold-starts are the worst. Can Redwood pre-warm KV cache before the run?
[02:40] Ethan Ross: yep, we can schedule a pre-warm pass; the trick is TTL and invalidation when you roll models. For the POC we used a scripted pre-warm that runs a curated prompt set which reduced cold latency by ~120 ms on average.
[02:54] Priya Shah: any risk of exposing PII in pre-warm? We need to be careful.
[02:58] Maya Chen: good flag. For pre-warm use sanitized prompts or synthetic prefixes; don't include PHI. We'll share the sanitized prompt set.
[03:08] Alex Rivera: can we get the sanitized list today?
[03:11] Maya Chen: yes, we'll attach it to the sheet after this call.
[03:15] [00:03:20] Ethan Ross: jumping back to the quantization experiments — we ran a 4-bit quantize on the midline model and saw 1.9x throughput improvement but slight fuzz in outputs on a small evaluation set. Not catastrophic, but we need to check your fidelity criteria.
[03:33] Michael Ortiz: what does "fuzz" mean exactly? Like more hallucinations or degraded token overlap?
[03:38] Ethan Ross: primarily reduced token-level KL for very rare tokens -> sometimes shorter completions or slightly different phrasing. For typical Crownline prompts the downstream classifier still passed.
[03:48] Sara Nguyen: classifier pass is good but product wants no change to critical labels. We can run a focused eval with your eval harness.
[03:55] Ethan Ross: perfect — we can run quant test with your eval set. We'll tag results with accuracy deltas.
[04:01] [00:04:20] Priya Shah: network question — earlier you mentioned routing policies, can Redwood route by region and failover to hosted in case dedicated is saturated?
[04:09] Maya Chen: yes the smart router can route by region, cost tier, or latency. If a dedicated pool is saturated, we can failover to a compatible hosted model variant automatically, configurable by SLO thresholds.
[04:21] Alex Rivera: what about data isolation? We need to ensure logs and prompts don't go to shared indexes for regulated workloads.
[04:27] Maya Chen: for Dedicated we offer isolated storage and can disable cross-customer indexing. For Private we can give you a customer-managed control plane and KMS integration.
[04:35] Priya Shah: SOC 2 — timeline for a SOC2/ISO review? Our security folks will want to talk.
[04:41] Maya Chen: we can schedule a security deep-dive next week; I'll include our SOC 2 attestation and architecture doc. Alex, can you confirm availability?
[04:47] Alex Rivera: yes aim for next Thu morning, will check with security.
[04:51] [00:05:10] Michael Ortiz: back to anomalies — Ethan you mentioned p99 spikes. Do we have traces that show if it's KV miss or kernel fallback?
[05:00] Ethan Ross: we have traces, and in some spikes we saw a kernel selection path that used a fallback FP path (non-quantized) — that happens when the quantized kernel can't satisfy sequence length or when a rare op occurs. That fallback adds 200-400ms sometimes.
[05:16] Priya Shah: any mitigation for that?
[05:18] Ethan Ross: we can restrict routing so sequences that match a known pattern go to a safe path, or we can expand quantized kernel coverage with a compile pass. Both are doable; the compile pass takes extra validation time.
[05:31] [00:05:40] Sara Nguyen: is there a way to detect and auto-fallback without user-visible latency?
[05:36] Ethan Ross: auto-fallback inevitably costs latency. But we can add shadow routing to predict when a request will fallback and pre-route it. That's more complex but reduces visibility of fallback.
[05:47] Alex Rivera: interesting. For our timeline — two weeks to decide on production config. What do you recommend we do in the next week to get good data?
[05:55] Maya Chen: run a 1k qps window during their business hour with both routing configs: low-latency small-batch pool vs normal batch. We'll put tracing instrumentation, and Redwood will collect percentiles and kernel trace samples.
[06:08] Michael Ortiz: we can run a daytime test next Tue between 14:00-15:00 UTC.
[06:13] Maya Chen: perfect. Ethan will set up the test harness and provide runbook.
[06:18] [00:06:50] Ethan Ross: also doing the quantization runs on a copy of the model with your eval set. I'll include token overlap metrics and hallucination flags.
[06:27] Priya Shah: about cost — can you put a quick estimate of per-1000-token unit cost for the low-latency pool vs the normal pool? That will help product.
[06:35] Maya Chen: yes, I'll update the pricing sheet with unit economics and per-route estimate. That will show the incremental cost for p95 targets.
[06:44] Alex Rivera: one more thing — our incumbent OldVendorAI had a weird optimization that cached full responses for a set of templated prompts; any chance Redwood can do similar?
[06:53] Ethan Ross: yes, Redwood supports response-level caching for deterministic prompts. We can set a TTL and cache keys; for dynamic user prompts it's trickier.
[07:02] Sara Nguyen: we'll follow up with a list of templated prompts that are safe to cache.
[07:06] [00:07:20] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood to share updated latency spreadsheet, sanitized pre-warm prompts, pricing update. Ethan to run quant experiments and prepare runbook for 1k qps test next Tue. Alex to confirm SOC2 call availability. Action items in the sheet.
[07:28] Alex Rivera: great, that aligns. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[07:31] Ethan Ross: just validation time for the quant compile; should be fine within the week.
[07:35] Priya Shah: and we'll prep logs and access for the test.
[07:39] [00:07:50] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD with the artifacts.
[07:53] Michael Ortiz: thanks, bye.
[07:55] Alex Rivera: bye.
[07:56] [end]
